name: Joseph McCarthy
summary: Joseph McCarthy was a Wisconsin Republican senator who made combating communism the focus of his national political career. As chair of the Senate Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations, he pursued alleged Communist influence in government, the military and other institutions. He backed the North Atlantic Treaty and supported federal farm price supports.

abolish-armed-forces.rationale: McCarthy voted to strengthen the armed forces through S. 2655 and to authorize use of the military to defend Formosa (80th Senate roll 216 and 84th Senate roll 5).

abolish-income-tax.rationale: McCarthy voted for H.R. 1 to reduce individual income-tax payments while retaining the income tax (80th Senate roll 74).

abolish-rental-housing.rationale: McCarthy supported public and private rental housing through legislation, including his own amendment on eligibility for subsidized tenancies (81st Senate rolls 68 and 74).

annexed-territory-occupation.rationale: In S. Res. 116 McCarthy treated Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania as areas under Communist domination whose status remained unsettled. He opposed treating Soviet control as legally recognized and asked for the issue to be taken up at Geneva.

ban-extremist-parties.rationale: McCarthy voted for the Humphrey substitute to outlaw the Communist Party and for the final conference report on that legislation (83rd Senate rolls 240 and 255, August 1954).

ban-interest.rationale: McCarthy voted to retain federal loan provisions in S. 1070 that financed low-income farm housing through repayable loans with interest (81st Senate roll 66).

collective-defense.rationale: McCarthy voted to ratify the North Atlantic Treaty, whose Article 5 treats an armed attack against one party as an attack against all (81st Senate roll 128, July 21, 1949).

conscription.rationale: McCarthy voted for S. 2655 in 1948 after supporting an amendment that would shorten the period of involuntary induction from 24 to 18 months (80th Senate rolls 212 and 216).

defeat-communism.rationale: McCarthy introduced S. Res. 116 urging the United States to make discussion of Communist control in Eastern Europe and Asia a condition of the Geneva summit agenda. The resolution argued that lasting U.S. security required an end to that control.

direct-election-head-of-state.rationale: McCarthy voted for Langer’s proposal to elect the president by nationwide popular vote in 1950. In 1956 he voted against two direct-election proposals and supported giving the states a choice of ways to allocate electoral votes (84th Senate rolls 131–134).

elective-rulers.rationale: McCarthy voted for constitutional proposals to elect the president directly in 1950 and to revise the system of presidential electors in 1956 (84th Senate roll 134).

end-foreign-alliances.rationale: McCarthy voted to ratify the North Atlantic Treaty and opposed a reservation limiting the United States’ obligations under its mutual-defense article (81st Senate rolls 126 and 128).

expand-fossil-fuels.rationale: McCarthy voted for the conference report on H.R. 5134, the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act of 1953, which authorized the federal government to issue new offshore oil and gas leases (83rd Senate roll 90).

farm-price-support.rationale: In 1954 McCarthy proposed parity price supports of 90 to 100 percent for basic crops, and in 1956 he voted for the farm bill conference report containing mandatory 90 percent supports for a year (83rd Senate roll 222 and 84th Senate roll 136).

force-without-un.rationale: McCarthy voted to authorize the president to use U.S. armed forces to protect Formosa and related territories under H.J. Res. 159, which did not require Security Council approval (84th Senate roll 5).

free-trade.rationale: On July 14, 1949, McCarthy argued that free trade can help countries with comparable wages but that unrestricted competition with very low-wage producers would lower American wages and living standards (Senate speeches 810098526 and 810098581).

independent-nuclear-deterrent.rationale: McCarthy defended continued American production and retention of atomic weapons against a proposal to stop production and dispose of the material (Senate speeches 810248904 and 820116398).

keep-nuclear-weapons.rationale: In Senate speeches on June 2, 1950 and August 20, 1951, McCarthy criticized the proposal to end American atomic bomb production and dispose of U.S. weapons material while confronting the Soviet Union (speeches 810248904 and 820116398).

military-force-beyond-defence.rationale: McCarthy voted to authorize U.S. military force to protect Formosa and related territories (84th Senate roll 5, January 28, 1955).

national-law-over-international.rationale: McCarthy voted for an amendment stipulating that a treaty could be supreme law only if made in pursuance of the Constitution (83rd Senate roll 103, February 18, 1954).

night-watchman-state.rationale: McCarthy introduced a federal farm price-support amendment and voted for amendments maintaining subsidized low-income housing (83rd Senate roll 222 and 81st Senate rolls 66 and 68).

one-party-rule.rationale: McCarthy argued in Milwaukee that the United States could not long endure under a one-party system. In McCarthyism: The Fight for America he called for members of both major parties to join the campaign against communism.

politics-spiritual-struggle.rationale: In his Wheeling address McCarthy cast the Cold War as a struggle between atheistic communism and Christianity and called for a moral renewal to stop alleged betrayal at home.

price-controls-essentials.rationale: During the postwar sugar shortage McCarthy offered and voted for an amendment retaining federal sugar price controls and rationing through October 1947 while shortening their proposed duration (80th Senate roll 30).

racial-segregation-law.rationale: McCarthy voted for a ban on racial discrimination in occupancy of federally supported low-income housing and against providing for racially segregated enlistment units (81st Senate rolls 62, 63 and 362).

restrict-strikes-picketing.rationale: McCarthy voted to outlaw jurisdictional strikes and secondary boycotts in 1947 and voted in 1952 to ask the president to invoke the Taft-Hartley emergency provisions in the steel strike (80th Senate roll 53 and 82nd Senate roll 273).

restrict-technology-exports-to-rivals.rationale: McCarthy voted to bar American aid to countries that knowingly permitted exports of war material to the Communist bloc (82nd Senate roll 238).

separated-powers.rationale: McCarthy introduced S. Res. 116 asserting congressional responsibility alongside the executive in foreign policy and voted for the Bricker amendment proposal limiting when treaties could take effect as domestic law (83rd Senate rolls 105 and 109).

state-directs-investment.rationale: McCarthy voted for H.R. 9176, the Defense Production Act of 1950, which allowed the federal government to finance expansion of productive capacity for national defense (81st Senate roll 413).

state-harmful.rationale: McCarthy used the Senate’s investigative authority to question witnesses about alleged subversion and voted to grant military induction powers and fund agricultural price supports.

stay-neutral-between-blocs.rationale: McCarthy voted for the United States to join the North Atlantic alliance in 1949 (81st Senate roll 128).

tariffs-protect-industry.rationale: McCarthy voted in 1955 to retain the trade agreement safeguards through which domestic industries injured by imports could obtain tariff protection (84th Senate roll 34). In 1949 he offered an amendment to the Tariff Act to protect domestic fur producers from import competition (81st Senate rolls 181 and 184).

unlimited-reelection.rationale: McCarthy voted for passage of H.J. Res. 27, the proposed Twenty-Second Amendment to limit presidential reelection (80th Senate roll 19, March 12, 1947).

women-suffrage.rationale: McCarthy voted for the 1950 Equal Rights Amendment, which would guarantee equal legal rights regardless of sex while preserving existing statutory protections for women (81st Senate rolls 235 and 237).

notes: Checked Voteview roll calls and the Stanford Congressional Record for economic policy, legal protections, government institutions, foreign policy, race and religion, resource policy, and atomic technology. Also reviewed the two published books, the Wheeling address as entered in the Senate record, and the Senate investigation transcripts for McCarthy’s views on political methods and culture. Follow-up searches covered monarchism and election rules, sex equality and family policy, local government, Indigenous jurisdiction, secession and autonomy, environmental limits, nuclear power, religion, and legislative checks. Some signature positions concern loyalty investigations and federal employment, where the record is more specific than the corresponding quiz topics.
